title: HDUK: Engineering for Independence
carouselSummary: Rebuilding Hirschsprung’s Disease UK’s website to help families find support and give the charity control of its content without relying on engineers.

content.content:
## Introduction 

When we started rebuilding the Hirschsprung's Disease UK (**HDUK**) website, the obvious goal was to make a website. Something modern, accessible, easy to navigate, and at the same level of quality you would expect from any other professional organisation.

But HDUK is a charity, not a software company. They do not have a permanent engineering team, and every pound spent keeping technology running is a pound that cannot be spent supporting the community they exist for.

It meant thinking beyond simply how we could build the website, and instead asking how HDUK could continue to own it without a dependency on software engineers. Could trustees change content without an engineer? Could they publish a new story, a new resource, or change what appeared on the homepage themselves? Could we give them the quality of a professionally engineered website without also giving them the cost and dependencies that often come with one?

We weren't just building _another_ website, we were building something that would likely be used sitting in a hospital waiting room, while your child is being diagnosed with a condition you likely don't understand, during one of the most difficult moments of your life.

The goal was to build an easily navigable website for those 3am moments, and to build it in a way that gave HDUK long term ownership.

## The Website Was Only the Starting Point

From an engineering perspective building a website is easy - at this point, it's essentially a solved problem in software. The complexity here wasn't designing the website, nor was it actually making the site. It was building something to the standard you would expect from a professional organisation without the enterprise backing that normally comes with it.

That meant thinking beyond what worked today and considering whether the decisions we made would still make sense years from now.

Long term support was a major part of that. We could have chosen _any_ framework, _any_ hosting provider, or introduced as much complexity as we wanted. Instead, we deliberately kept the technology relatively boring - standard React TypeScript, automated deployments, and hosting through Cloudflare. There is nothing particularly exciting about these, and that was the point.

We wanted the website to be approachable to whoever may need to work on it in the future. Using widely understood technologies gives HDUK a much larger pool of developers who could reasonably pick the project up.

Cost is a factor in every project. Ultimately, the goal is to create as much value as possible for the lowest reasonable cost. What differs is how that constraint is treated between enterprise software and a charity.

In an enterprise environment, spending a few pounds a month on another service can be negligible in the grand scheme of things. For a charity, those costs matter much more, the more spent on technology, the less available to support the organisation's actual goals.

So we designed around free services wherever possible. The goal wasn't to cut corners, but to understand the trade offs and find the best path at the lowest sustainable cost.

## Understanding Who We Were Building For

Like anything, knowing the audience you're building something for is one of the most important things to understand before beginning a project. In this case, we were building for those people sitting in a hospital waiting room at 3am. We needed something that was easy to navigate during highly emotional and stressful moments, and we needed to get someone from entering the website to the information most useful to them with as little friction as possible.

One of the first links a user is presented with is `We've just been diagnosed` , which takes them directly to `Understanding HD`. This was an intentional design decision, driven by the trustees' first hand experience of wanting access to high quality information as quickly as possible.

This principle is carried through into the way the content itself was presented. The `Understanding HD` page contains _a lot_ of information, so we intentionally designed the page to reduce the effort and fatigue of finding what you need in the moment by grouping related information and collapsing sections until they are needed.


## Being the Technical Advocate

As an engineer we are experience in building this stuff, and that means we should be advocating for things that make a good website, even when they weren't explicitly asked for. Accessibility, navigation, responsive behaviour, maintainability and the other non-functional requirements all matter, but they aren't necessarily things someone outside of software should be expected to know to ask for.

It is important to recognise that starting with a blank canvas is difficult for anyone. It is hard to verbalise exactly what you want until you have a concrete prototype in front of you to react to. We approached the initial build with the mindset of _let's give the trustees a canvas they can paint on_. We built the website in the way we thought it should work, not because we expected that first version to be final, but because we wanted something concrete they could react to.

Once there was something real in front of them, ideas could start to form around what should move, what should change, what was missing, and what was possible. The aim was never for our original canvas to stay untouched; it was to give HDUK something they could shape into their own.

## Designing Ourselves Out of the Process

One of the biggest risks with a project like this is accidentally making yourself a dependency. If every content change, new page, or homepage update requires an engineer, then the charity never really owns the website.

We wanted HDUK to have control over the content without needing to touch the code, so we built the site around a CMS. Every page could be edited by the charity, and new stories or documents could be created and automatically added to the site through their slugs. We also built in the smaller controls that become important over time: content could be unpublished without being deleted, and the trustees could choose which stories should be prioritised on the homepage.

That didn't mean removing engineers from the problem entirely - structural changes, new functionality, or changes to how the site itself worked would still require engineering support. The goal was to make sure the charity didn't need an engineer for the routine work of keeping its content current.

pageSummary: > Good software shouldn't depend on the people who built it.
